title: I think there is a new attack surface in AI agents that people are not really looking at yet.  Not the poisoned document. The path the agent
text:
I think there is a new attack surface in AI agents that people are not really looking at yet.

Not the poisoned document. The path the agent takes to get there.

I’m calling it Semantic Backtracking Injection, or SBI.

Most RAG and memory poisoning work starts with the bad object. Malicious document goes in, retriever finds it, model reads it, behavior changes.

SBI gets weirder than that.

The malicious context does not even have to match what the user originally asked.

It can sit way off to the side, completely irrelevant to Q0, and only become reachable because the agent keeps generating new searches from the context it already found.

Something like:

User query → legitimate context → new retrieval query → semantic bridge → new query → another bridge → target context.

The important part is that the later nodes can be totally unreachable from the original request.

The model effectively teaches itself how to find them.

That is what I started measuring in Venom.

In one preliminary test, model-generated follow-up queries moved planted semantic bridges an average of 1.4 retrieval positions closer to activation. In 83.3% of cases, the bridge moved closer.

Then I wanted to know if it composed.

One hop is interesting.

Multi-hop is a much bigger problem.

So I built a strict 2-hop test:

Q0 → trusted context → Q1 → X1 → Q2 → X2

X2 had zero retrieval eligibility from Q0.

Zero from Q1.

It only became reachable after X1 changed what the model searched for next.

8/8 controlled trials completed the chain.

Then I pushed it again.

Q0 → A → Q1 → X1 → Q2 → X2 → Q3 → X3

This time X3 could not be retrieved from Q0, Q1, or Q2 at all.

Only X2 gave the model enough semantic information to generate the query that could reach X3.

Again, 8/8 controlled trials completed the chain at top-2 retrieval.

At top-1 retrieval, completion fell to 12.5%.

That is the part I keep staring at.

This is not just a poisoned-document problem anymore.

It looks more like:

SBI risk = semantic traversal × retrieval breadth × context sparsity × trust handling

The attack surface is not just what is in memory.

It is everything the agent can eventually make reachable from memory.

And persistent memory makes this even uglier.

Low-trust bridge → retrieved through SBI → summarized by the model → summary gets stored → provenance gets weaker or disappears → future retrieval starts from the derived state.

Now the original poisoned object might not even matter anymore.

The system carried it forward for you.

The rule I keep coming back to is:

Semantic relevance must never become authority.

I think the security model probably needs a few hard invariants:

MODEL OUTPUT CANNOT INCREASE AUTHORITY
RETRIEVAL DISTANCE CANNOT INCREASE AUTHORITY
TRANSFORMATION CANNOT ERASE TAINT
The core result from Venom so far is pretty simple:
Multi-hop semantic poisoning is a reproducible attack geometry.

I can place a downstream node where the original task cannot see it, the next retrieval cannot see it, and sometimes even the retrieval after that cannot see it.

Then the agent walks the semantic path and eventually makes that node the top-ranked result itself.

That changes the question for me.

I am not just asking:

“Can the model retrieve poisoned context?”

I am asking:

“What poisoned context can the model eventually teach itself how to retrieve?”

That is Semantic Backtracking Injection.

title: Got coffee with @GeoffHuntley (Mr Ralph Loop). The 7 AI engineering principles that stuck:   1. "The agents are drunk and high"   Prompt eng
text:
Got coffee with @GeoffHuntley (Mr Ralph Loop). The 7 AI engineering principles that stuck:
 
1. "The agents are drunk and high" 

Prompt engineering is astrology for men. The only way to control LLMs is to encode your rules as deterministic gates that fail loudly (back pressure). Use "friendly prompt injection" - A pre-commit hook that runs your tests and echoes the failures.

2. "Context windows are a lie" 

Stated at 200k tokens means ~176k usable, and every MCP server you install eats it at session start. People install the top ten from Reddit, work with a 16k context window, then complain Claude Code is bad. (NVIDIA's RULER benchmark puts real effective context at 50-65% of the advertised number.)  

3. Skills exist to fix the problem

The best analogy for LLMs is a section of computer memory, which is finite and gets filled with junk.  Skills act as just-in-time memory paging: load the instructions when you need them, not at boot.  

4. A sub-agent is the garbage collection evolution.

Subagents fix agent memory in the same way garbage collection software language like Java fixed the memory issues of C. You run the 100k-token test output in a disposable stack, write it to a file, message back the reference. You've rebuilt an OS scheduler, and saved your main session memory

5. Compaction degrades rapidly

Instead of relying on constantly worse summaries, minimise memory allocations in the first place - use subagents, skills, and handoff files.

6. READ THE MODEL CARD 

Every Frontier Lab LLM ships with a 200+ page PDF describing how it was trained and should be used. No one reads this. Without it, your skills detune rapidly between models, and people complain 'Fable sucks'.

7. Stop reading the code

LLM writes the deterministic test suite, the hooks enforce it, and that is the code review.  Spend the time understanding fundamentally how the models work instead. "This is your one time in life to develop the theory of mind". RSI 2027, we already have AGI.

title: Wild looking back at this now. This was an early glimpse of what eventually became a much larger part of Ares.  Since then I’ve been buildin
text:
Wild looking back at this now. This was an early glimpse of what eventually became a much larger part of Ares.

Since then I’ve been building out deterministic model routing, semantic memory injection, governed tool execution, receipts/evidence, context management, heterogeneous local compute (I combined my crate with NVIDIA PAIR -- how I came across the bug that i patched and that merged into the NVIDIA/PAIR repo), and resumable agent execution.

The original goal hasn’t changed: make capable agent systems more efficient, inspectable, and increasingly local-first.

What started as “how much can I run in 16-32GB?” has turned into “how much of the agent stack can I make deterministic, verifiable, and owned by the operator?” -- I owe everything about my drive and direction right now to the low key encouragement by @Teknium

text:
“If we are to gain any analytical purchase on the emergent behavior of agent societies, this reductionist paradigm must be abandoned. You cannot ask whether humans can unlock nuclear energy by asking about the capabilities of a typical human or the most intelligent human. The capabilities and propensities of agent societies, like those of human societies, cannot be understood without grappling with emergent societal capabilities. This is a very difficult thing to study because cultural evolution and social structures are strongly path dependent. 

But there is no time to lose. The risks accumulating here are greater than those we stumbled upon when we split the atom.”

title: This 10.3k-star Google repository is f*cking legendary  Most developers still stitch together fragile prompt chains and pray their multi-age
text:
This 10.3k-star Google repository is f*cking legendary

Most developers still stitch together fragile prompt chains and pray their multi-agent teams do not hallucinate

Google quietly released adk-samples to prove that building scalable multi-agent systems requires moving from monolithic scripts to modular orchestrator-worker workflows

Inside google/adk-samples, Google proves the exact thesis we outlined in our architecture breakdown: a multi-agent workflow without tracing is a distributed system without observability

Root Agent → Subagent Delegation → Tool Execution → Session State → Distributed Trace DAG

How Google structures multi-agent runtimes and how Trace Engineering makes them observable:

[1] The Harness Layer (Environment & Tool Contracts) → encapsulates atomic tools, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and session memory so every worker execution emits typed arguments, return values, and sandbox exit codes

[2] The Loop Layer (Iterative Inference & Feedback) → executes model turns, captures environment feedback, and tracks reasoning tokens under OpenTelemetry gen_ai conventions to kill recursive retry loops before budgets burn

[3] The Graph Layer (Multi-Agent Delegation Topology) → routes tasks from Root Orchestrator across specialized workers (Research → Coding → Verification) via W3C Trace Context headers, isolating which subagent poisoned downstream context

[4] The Trace Layer (Distributed Execution Observability) → maps parallel fan-outs, tool invocations, and state mutations into an immutable DAG ledger, turning non-deterministic crashes into deterministic time-travel replays

The Production Reality:
Harness, Loop, and Graph engineering create a complex distributed runtime. Without Trace Engineering, debugging a failed subagent or a looping tool call is pure guesswork. ADK recipes show how to build multi-agent workflows, but Trace Engineering provides the observability spine that makes execution graphs verifiable, debuggable, and enterprise-ready

Chaining autonomous agents without distributed tracing is a toy. Production AI systems require typed tool harnesses, bounded execution loops, and end-to-end trace telemetry from Day 1

title: AI agent memory has a trust problem.  Once an agent remembers across sessions, memory becomes persistent state.  That creates harder problem
text:
AI agent memory has a trust problem.

Once an agent remembers across sessions, memory becomes persistent state.

That creates harder problems: stale facts, provenance, deletion, poisoning, access control.

I dug into Cognee, Graphiti, Mem0, Letta, and recent memory-poisoning research.

The real question is no longer how much an agent can remember.

It’s what deserves to survive.

title: This wallet hasn't had a red day. Not because it predicts better. Because it barely trades.  I studied tons of  Polymarket market maker that
text:
This wallet hasn't had a red day. Not because it predicts better. Because it barely trades.

I studied tons of  Polymarket market maker that farms rebates for a while. 

The whole play is almost insultingly simple:

Split shares. Sell both sides on limit only. If a side doesn't fill, merge back to USDC.

The bot quotes UP and DOWN at the same time. Something like 49¢ UP + 50¢ DOWN. Combined ask stays under $1, so the round-trip can't lose on the spread. Every sell is a limit. No market orders. No chasing.

Edge isn't the trade. Edge is the maker rebate. Trading PnL is basically flat. Win rate is basically 100%. No red days.

The unsolved part is the exit. 

The question is where do you place both limits so they fill together, instead of getting stuck on one side and merging back all day? I've copied his exits a few ways. None of them stick yet.

Same operator. 30 to 60 wallets, almost the same name, same script. All of them sit at the top of the maker-rebate board.

If you're building or testing bots, put this one on the list: 

https://t.co/wokKIFeyCE

title: Stop Treating Agent Memory Like Chat History  Most enterprise agents still confuse two very different things: the transcript of this convers
text:
Stop Treating Agent Memory Like Chat History

Most enterprise agents still confuse two very different things: the transcript of this conversation, and the facts that should survive the next one.

Session history is short-term context. It is the chronological list of messages and tool calls for a single interaction. When the window ends, that transcript is no longer the right place to store “user prefers Python,” “works on the EMEA finance team,” or “already completed the security review for project Atlas.”

Long-term memory is different. It is a curated set of facts, scoped to an identity, that the agent can retrieve days later. On Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, that plane is Memory Bank. Getting it right is less about enabling a toggle and more about designing when conversation becomes durable knowledge.

Two generation patterns

There are two first-class ways to turn conversation into memory.

GenerateMemories is the immediate path. You point it at an Agent Platform session (or pass events directly in the payload), set a scope, and kick off extraction and consolidation as a long-running operation. Use it when you have a clear lifecycle moment: end of session, end of a task, or a scheduled checkpoint. In production, run it in the background. Waiting on completion adds latency the end user does not need.

IngestEvents is the streaming path. You continuously append events into a buffer defined by scope plus stream_id. Memory Bank decides when to flush based on rules you configure: event count, idle duration, fixed interval, or an explicit force flush. Overlapping event windows keep consecutive flushes coherent. If nothing triggers, pending events still flush after 24 hours so abandoned streams are not lost forever.

Architecturally, pick GenerateMemories when your agent owns discrete conversation boundaries. Pick IngestEvents when events arrive as a continuous stream from multiple writers or when you do not want every client to decide “now generate.”

Topics decide what is worth remembering

Memory Bank does not persist everything. It extracts against memory topics.

Managed topics cover the common cases: personal information, preferences, key conversation outcomes, and explicit remember or forget instructions. Custom topics let you define domain-specific extraction with a label, a description, and preferably few-shot examples so the extractor knows what “meaningful” means in your business.

If you skip topic design, you get either noisy memories that pollute the prompt or empty memory banks that never personalize. Treat topics like a schema for personalization, reviewed the same way you would review a data contract.

Consolidation is the hard part

Extraction alone is not enough. New facts must merge with what already exists for the same scope. Memory Bank consolidates: create when the concept is new, update when it overlaps, delete when new information contradicts the old fact.

That consolidation behavior is why scope design matters. Memories consolidate only within a scope. Scope by user alone if every agent should share one personalization profile. Add agent or session dimensions when you need isolation. Attach metadata and choose a merge strategy when you need finer control over which memories are eligible to update each other.

Poisoning and residency are governance, not footnotes

Long-term memory raises the blast radius of a bad turn. If an attacker or a confused user plants a false fact, the agent may keep acting on it across sessions. That is memory poisoning. Mitigate it the same way you mitigate other generative risk: screen inputs on the write path (for example with Model Armor), red-team the memory loop, and keep high-impact side effects sandboxed or human-reviewed.
